blocks.recap_md: The chapter opens with Locke's epigraph on the mind's three acts: combining, comparing, and abstracting simple ideas into complex ones.
Programs are framed as 'spells' that conjure computational processes, like a sorcerer's spirit - precise and powerful, but small bugs can have large, unanticipated consequences.
Real-world programming demands care and expertise; master engineers build systems modularly, so parts can be constructed, replaced, and debugged separately.

knowledge_items.statement: The chapter frames programs as 'spells' that conjure computational processes (like a sorcerer's spirit) to manipulate data - vivid language for the fact that a process executes its program precisely and mechanically, so small bugs can have significant, unanticipated consequences.

Well-designed computational systems, like well-designed physical systems, are built in a modular manner so that parts can be constructed, replaced, and debugged separately - managing complexity through this kind of structure is a central theme of the book.

questions.prompt: The chapter's opening compares programs to a sorcerer's spells and computational processes to the spirits they conjure. What is this analogy mainly meant to convey?
options: That a computational process executes the program that directs it precisely and mechanically, so small errors (bugs) can have significant, unanticipated real-world consequences
That programming is inherently more dangerous than any other engineering discipline
That computers are literally unpredictable and cannot be reasoned about in advance
That only expert 'sorcerers' should be allowed to write programs
questions.explanation: The text draws the parallel to make exactly this point: a computational process executes its program precisely and accurately, so even small bugs can have complex, unanticipated consequences - which is why real-world programming demands care, expertise, and wisdom.

questions.prompt: According to the text, why do master software engineers design computational systems in a modular manner?
options: So that the parts can be constructed, replaced, and debugged separately, similar to well-designed automobiles or nuclear reactors
Because modular programs always run faster than non-modular ones
Because most programming languages require modularity as a syntax rule
So that only one engineer ever needs to understand the whole system
questions.explanation: The text draws a direct analogy to well-designed physical systems: modularity lets the parts of a program be constructed, replaced, and debugged separately - a hallmark of being able to visualize and control a system's behavior in advance.
